power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = 1.0 ", "p = 2.4 "), Sentence = c("MAVE trafficking scores reported previously 11 for the 73 variants common to both datasets (Pearson r = 0.804, R² = 0.647, p = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁷; Spearman ρ = 0.685, p = 2.4 × 10⁻¹¹; Figure S3f).", "MAVE trafficking scores reported previously 11 for the 73 variants common to both datasets (Pearson r = 0.804, R² = 0.647, p = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁷; Spearman ρ = 0.685, p = 2.4 × 10⁻¹¹; Figure S3f)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Background: The increasing use of genetic testing has identified thousands of KCNH2 variants associated with long QT syndrome type 2 (LQT2), yet most remain variants of uncertain significance (VUS).
Translating functional abnormalities into clinically actionable evidence remains a major challenge.
We established a nationwide functional genomics strategy to systematically characterize KCNH2 variants identified in the French LQT2 population and improve their clinical interpretation.
Methods: We characterized 303 KCNH2 variants, including 201 VUS, using standardized highthroughput automated patch-clamp electrophysiology and complementary membrane trafficking assays.
Nine electrophysiological parameters were integrated using MeTAL to predict variant-specific repolarization phenotypes under homozygous and heterozygous conditions.
Modeled QTc values were compared with patient electrocardiographic data and variant-specific penetrance estimates.
Functional evidence was calibrated against established benign and pathogenic variants using ClinGenrecommended categorical OddsPath and continuous likelihood-ratio approaches.
Results: Multidimensional functional profiling revealed abnormalities not captured by current amplitude alone, identifying additional variants with clinically relevant repolarization defects.

Among variants assessed under heterozygous conditions, MeTAL predictions showed 82.9% concordance with patient QTc phenotypes for ACMG class 5 variants, with apparent discordances partly consistent with incomplete penetrance.
Continuous likelihood-ratio calibration demonstrated strong discrimination between established benign and pathogenic variants (AUC=0.936) and provided graded functional evidence for 76.1% of VUS.

Integration of calibrated functional evidence into the ACMG/AMP framework enabled reclassification of 64 of 201 VUS (31.8%), including 7 as pathogenic, 46 as likely pathogenic, and 11 as likely benign.

Conclusions: This nationwide study establishes a scalable framework integrating high-throughput electrophysiology, computational modeling, and clinical phenotyping to translate complex KCNH2 channel dysfunction into clinically interpretable evidence.
The resulting reclassification of nearly onethird of VUS, together with the open-access HAMMER database, provides a resource to improve molecular diagnosis and risk assessment in LQT2.

Variants of KCNH2, the gene encoding the cardiac hERG potassium channel, have been implicated in congenital Long QT Syndrome type 2 (LQT2) and Short QT syndrome type 1 (SQT1), rare inherited arrhythmic disorders characterized by delayed or abbreviated ventricular repolarization and an increased risk of sudden cardiac death [1] [2] [3] [4] .

text.text: Although functional interpretation of VUS has historically lagged behind the pace of variant discovery, coordinated international initiatives are now addressing this gap.

text.text: These initiatives represent an important step toward translating variant detection into clinically relevant interpretation.
Despite their considerable value, these approaches remain subject to important limitations.
First, electrophysiological studies lack standardized experimental protocols, making direct and reliable comparisons across studies challenging 8 .

text.text: Second, because KCNH2-related disorders are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, expression systems that strictly ensure equal expression of the wildtype (WT) and variant alleles are essential for accurately assessing variant pathogenicity in the heterozygous state.
Third, functional analyses often focus on a restricted subset of biophysical parameters 11, 16 .

text.text: Although hERG channel expression is an established determinant of channel function and disease risk, our recent systematic investigation demonstrated that other biophysical parameters, including channel inactivation, also play a role in determining the pathogenicity of individual variants 17 .

text.text: Assessing channel conductance alone therefore fails to capture the full spectrum of functionally relevant properties and may lead to inaccurate estimates of the clinical pathogenicity of hERG VUS.
Indeed, alterations in other hERG channel biophysical properties may either exacerbate or compensate for the pathogenic effects of altered channel expression levels.

Individual variants often produce a mixture of gain-(GoF) and loss-of-function (LoF) features, rendering their clinical interpretation particularly challenging in the absence of an integrative analytical framework 18 .

text.text: To address this complexity, we previously developed MeTAL 17 , a computational package specifically designed to integrate the full spectrum of hERG biophysical properties that provides QTc evaluations as clinicallyrelevant assessment of variant pathogenicity.

text.text: MeTAL establishes a rationale linking channel phenotypes -including gating kinetics and voltage-dependence for activation, inactivation, recovery from inactivation and deactivation besides current density -to patient-level clinical manifestations.

text.text: We further applied MeTAL as a binary classifier to identify functionally disruptive variants under homozygous conditions across all ACMG classes and subsequently to assess their predicted impact on ventricular repolarization under strict heterozygous conditions.
Using this systematic and standardized approach, we stratified the pathogenicity of French KCNH2 VUS, including variants for which channel expression was preserved.
Whenever clinical data were available, MeTAL-based pathogenicity predictions were compared with electrocardiographic phenotypes from patients carrying the corresponding variants.

Functional phenotypes were subsequently calibrated against established benign and pathogenic reference variants according to ClinGen recommendations, enabling the assignment of PS3/BS3 evidence strength for clinical variant interpretation.
Integration of this functional evidence into the ACMG/AMP classification framework supported the reclassification of 58 VUS as likely pathogenic.

Building on these complementary functional, computational, and clinical efforts, we established an open-access, web-based database integrating detailed genetic, clinical, functional, and patient-level data for all 303 variants.

This resource provides a comprehensive systematic characterization of KCNH2 VUS undertaken at the scale of a national cohort and represents an important step toward resolving the clinical interpretation and management of KCNH2 VUS.

text.text: The objective of this analysis was to determine whether incorporation of the functional evidence generated in the present study was sufficient to resolve the original VUS classification.
For each variant, the ACMG/AMP evidence criteria underlying the original classification were retrieved and retained at their previously assigned strength.
Pre-existing functional evidence (PS3 or BS3), when present, was excluded before recalculation to avoid double counting with the newly generated functional evidence.

The remaining evidence criteria were converted into points according to the naturally scaled system of Tavtigian et al. 23 : pathogenic supporting, moderate, strong, and very strong evidence contributed +1, +2, +4, and +8 points, respectively, whereas benign supporting, moderate, and strong evidence contributed -1, -2, and -4 points, respectively (Tables S5 and S6).

text.text: The resulting sum was considered the baseline non-functional evidence score for each variant.

New functional evidence obtained from MeTAL-modeled QTc was incorporated according to the ClinGen Sequence Variant Interpretation Working Group recommendations for application of the PS3/BS3 criteria 10 , using two calibration approaches.
In the categorical OddsPath-based approach, the strength of functional evidence was assigned on the basis of the previously determined OddsPath values.

Accordingly, variants displaying a deleterious functional phenotype were assigned PS3_moderate (+2 points), whereas variants displaying a functionally normal phenotype were assigned BS3_moderate (-2 points).

In parallel, continuous LLR calibration was used to assign variant-specific functional evidence strengths, ranging from supporting to very strong for pathogenic evidence (PS3: +1, +2, +4, or +8 points) and from supporting to strong for benign evidence (BS3: -1, -2, or -4 points).

Variants falling within the uninformative LLR interval received no additional functional evidence, while variants displaying SQT-like phenotypes were not assigned LLR-based evidence because the calibration was not applicable to QT shortening.

For each of the 201 VUS, final point scores were calculated independently for the OddsPath-and LLRbased approaches by algebraically summing the baseline non-functional evidence score and the corresponding newly assigned functional evidence points.
Final classification was determined using the Tavtigian et al. 23 thresholds: benign (≤-7 points), likely benign (-6 to -1), VUS (0 to 5), likely pathogenic (6 to 9), and pathogenic (≥10 points).

Calibration of MeTAL-modeled QTc for functional evidence assignment -To establish the strength of functional evidence according to the ClinGen Sequence Variant Interpretation (SVI) recommendations 10 , MeTAL-modeled QTc values were calibrated using variants with definitive ACMG classifications.

Rather than selecting variants according to their location within the channel or their prior classification, we Comparisons with previously published functional datasets highlight the importance of integrating multiple biophysical properties when interpreting KCNH2 variants.

Discrepancies across platforms may arise from differences in experimental conditions, particularly WT-to-variant expression ratios, but also reflect the limitations of approaches relying primarily on current amplitude or trafficking measurements.
Indeed, alterations in gating properties may reinforce or compensate for changes in current density, ultimately modifying their impact on ventricular repolarization.

By integrating these combined effects into a modeled QTc phenotype, MeTAL provides a complementary framework for refining functional evidence and emphasizes the importance of orthogonal validation in variant interpretation.
Variants were evaluated in two genotype contexts.

Homozygous expression measures the intrinsic capacity of a variant to perturb hERG function, whereas heterozygous expression reproduces the molecular context of LQT2 carriers and tests whether the defect persists in the presence of WT channels, where dominant-negative effects and allele dosage operate.

The two conditions were not interchangeable in our dataset: 69 variants showed a marked defect under homozygous conditions while retaining near-normal function in the heterozygous state, consistent with haploinsufficiency rather than dominant-negative suppression.

Extending this to patients, MeTAL predictions showed high patient-level concordance for class 5 variants (82.9%), and most apparent mismatches occurred for variants for which other carriers displayed the predicted phenotype, consistent with the incomplete penetrance of LQT2 and with recent large-scale penetrance analyses 11, 22 .

The relevance of such a comprehensive national strategy extends beyond the French cohort, as variants identified in France account for approximately 10% of KCNH2 variants currently reported in ClinVar, highlighting the substantial contribution of the French diagnostic network to the global landscape of KCNH2 variation.

This strategy provided functional evidence for all 201 VUS and, more broadly, established a standardized functional framework for 303 clinically identified variants.Beyond its scale, the principal advance of this study is the integration of standardized multiparametric electrophysiology, balanced (50%WT/50%variant) heterozygous functional assessment, MeTAL-based transformation of channel-level dysfunction into modeled repolarization phenotypes, and formal calibration of PS3/BS3 evidence.

This combination captures defects not detected by current amplitude alone, evaluates them in the genetic context of carriers, and translates complex and potentially opposing biophysical effects into clinically interpretable evidence.

To facilitate translation of these findings into clinical practice, we developed HAMMER, an open-access database integrating functional, computational, classification, and available clinical data for each variant.

By linking systematic experimental characterization with computational modeling and patient phenotypes, this approach provides a framework for connecting national genetic diagnostics with standardized functional interpretation.
More broadly, it illustrates how a clinically ascertained national cohort can serve as a framework for systematic functional genomics of an inherited ion-channel disorder.

Interpreted together, MeTAL and penetrance provide a framework for functionally stratifying VUS beyond their current class 3 designation and for placing individual patient QTc values within the phenotypic spectrum associated with each variant.Translating functional phenotypes into clinically usable evidence requires not only defining whether a variant is abnormal, but also quantifying the strength of that evidence.

The ClinGen Sequence Variant Interpretation Working Group specifically recommends calibration of well-established functional assays using known pathogenic and benign controls to determine the appropriate strength of PS3/BS3 evidence10 .

text.text: Calibration of MeTAL-modeled QTc according to this framework provided moderate PS3 or BS3 evidence across the complete dataset.
However, binary OddsPath classification necessarily assigns equivalent evidence strength to variants with substantially different degrees of functional alteration.
Taking advantage of the continuous nature of modeled QTc, our LLR calibration captured this magnitude and showed high discrimination between established benign and pathogenic variants (AUC = 0.936).

Importantly, this approach provided graded evidence toward pathogenicity or benignity for 76.1% of VUS, ranging from supporting to very strong evidence, while explicitly identifying variants for which the functional phenotype remained uninformative.
The clinical impact of this calibrated evidence is most apparent in the VUS category.
Prior functional evidence was available for only 2 of the 201 variants analyzed here.

By generating calibrated functional evidence across nearly the entire VUS dataset, our approach enabled 58 variants (28.9%) to be reclassified as likely pathogenic using categorical OddsPath calibration.

Importantly, continuous LLR calibration extended this contribution by enabling the reclassification of 64 variants (31.8%), including seven as pathogenic, 46 as likely pathogenic, and 11 as likely benign.

Although the overall reclassification rates were comparable, LLR calibration provided greater resolution of functional evidence strength, allowing variants to reach more definitive classifications in both pathogenic and benign directions.

This reclassification did not result from functional evidence acting in isolation, but from its quantitative integration with the preexisting evidence supporting each variant: most reclassified variants were already positioned close to the likely pathogenic threshold and crossed this boundary upon addition of PS3_moderate evidence.

The expression system, although standardized and highly scalable, does not reproduce the molecular and electrophysiological environment of human cardiomyocytes, and the controlled WT/variant context used to model heterozygosity may not reproduce all aspects of endogenous allele-specific expression, subunit assembly or cellular regulation.MeTAL is an intermediate computational representation of ventricular repolarization and pseudo-ECG modelling rather than a complete model of ventricular repolarization, and therefore cannot capture all interactions among cardiac ionic currents.

Clinical QTc is itself influenced by age, sex, heart rate, medications, autonomic state, and genetic and environmental modifiers, so a single ECG measurement may underestimate the functional contribution of a pathogenic variant.

These limitations reinforce rather than diminish the importance of integrating functional and clinical evidence.Together, our findings establish a scalable framework in which standardized multidimensional electrophysiology defines channel dysfunction and MeTAL translates this dysfunction into a clinically interpretable repolarization phenotype.

Continuous calibration then quantifies its evidentiary strength, allowing it to contribute directly to variant reclassification within the ACMG/AMP framework, while patient phenotypes and penetrance provide complementary clinical context.

Combined with open dissemination through HAMMER, this framework provides a direct path from high-throughput functional genomics to evidence-based interpretation of KCNH2 variants in patients and their families.
